An idea popped up as I was listening to the audio version of @IjeomaOluo's book, "So you want to talk about race."

White women in the #metoo movement say "believe the women." That is, allow women the authority to speak about their own experiences with rape, sexual assault...

The #blacklivesmatter movement also insists that their talk about their experiences with police brutality  [or "merely" threatened police brutality] and other aspects of racism be believed. That is, allow them the authority to speak about their own experiences with racism.

But more than a few white women in the #metoo movement refuse to see a parallel between women not being believed and POC not being believed.

Because accepting the authority of black women speaking about their experiences of racism within the #metoo movement [and elsewhere]...
Wow. Norm McDonald expresses sympathy for Louis CK while insulting Down's Syndrome people  while he thinks he is supporting #MeToo https://t.co/OzBesn9oWM

@jolisa_danielle @ToriBarron13 @brendddaboo @RealRomaDowney @EvelDick [Those stats flip dramatically, however, when a white woman accuses a black man. Because black men are believed even less than white women, and black women the least of all.]

Clearly you haven't the slightest notion of what #MeToo is all about.
@busywriting @JeffSharlet Hopefully these stats will change as the #metoo movement gains strength.

Clarifying: Black people are well aware of the potential danger police presence holds for them. & thoughtful white people are beginning to recognize that injustice as well.

We must not lose sight of the validity and seriousness of the concerns of the #BlackLivesMatter movement.

@dimplethomas @Ginger_Lyn_66 @PadmaLakshmi @InSpiteOfTrump @nytimes @kavita_krishnan @deepsealioness The fact that rape victims aren't charged with a crime should have no bearing on whether THEY have equal presumption of innocence.

When #MeToo says "believe the women," we say, give women the same presumption of innocence as the accused.
